::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Idea, 2026-10-02.** Nothing is built. Sections 3 to 5 are a first sketch,
and Section 6 lists what has to be decided before the first skill is written.
:::

## 1. Goal

Write a few skill files that an AI assistant loads before building or
evaluating a pharmacometrics model, so that its work follows the practice
already written down in published guidance and in internal guidance documents.

A skill here means a Markdown file of instructions, with a short description
that tells the assistant when to load it, in the format Claude Code and similar
tools read. One skill per task is the starting assumption: for example one for
building a population model, one for evaluating it, one for reporting it.

There is a lot of good guidance on this topic already, spread across
regulatory guidance, tutorials in *CPT: Pharmacometrics & Systems
Pharmacology*, and company-internal documents. None of it is in a form an
assistant loads before a task.

## 2. Out of Scope

- **Not a new guidance document.** The skills restate and cite guidance that
  exists. Where the sources disagree, the skill says so and names both.
- **Not a replacement for the modeler's judgment.** A skill sets the checks an
  assistant runs and reports; the modeler decides what a failed check means.
- **No unpublished internal material.** Internal guidance enters only as a
  checklist that has been cleared for publication.

## 3. Inputs

| # | Input | What it holds | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reference list | A couple of published sources per topic, the shortest set that covers it | First queue in [References](references.qmd) |
| 2 | Checklists | Internal guidance documents reduced to checklists that can be published | Not started; needs a clearance route |
| 3 | The skill files | The current version of each skill | Not started |

The reference list comes first, because it decides the topics. A first guess
at the topics: data assembly, structural model building, covariate modeling,
parameter estimation and its diagnostics, model evaluation including visual
predictive checks, simulation, and reporting.

## 4. The Yearly Rebuild

Most of the upkeep could be done by an AI assistant rebuilding each skill once
a year from four inputs.

1. The existing skill.
2. The curated references and checklists in Section 3.
3. A new literature review, asking for anything published since the last
   rebuild that should be included.
4. A separate review pass, by a second model or a set of agents, asking what
   is missing, wrong or out of date in the rebuilt skill.

The rebuild arrives as a pull request: a proposed change on GitHub that shows
every line added or removed, which the review group in Section 5 reads and
accepts or sends back. The literature review in step 3 also proposes additions
to the reference list, so the list grows through the same review.

## 5. Governance

The hard part is who decides what goes in. The proposal is to start with a
small, selective group: people who see the need, like working together and
respect each other's thinking. A wider group can come later, once a first
version exists for it to review.

GitHub carries most of the process. Anyone can open an issue or propose an
edit; the group merges.

The review schedule has two tiers, because a deep review every one, three or
five years is probably too slow on its own while the tools change this fast.

- **Every year.** The group reads the rebuild pull request from Section 4.
  This is a diff review, sized in hours.
- **Every three years, as a first guess.** The group re-reads the topics,
  the reference list and the checklists from scratch, and decides whether the
  set of skills itself should change.

## 6. Open Questions

1. **Which internal guidance documents exist, and who can clear a checklist
   drawn from one for publication?** This decides whether input 2 in Section 3
   is possible at all.
2. **Who is in the first review group?** Names, and how many.
3. **Where does the repository live?** A personal GitHub account, an
   organization created for it, or an existing society's account.
4. **How many skills, split how?** By task, as in Section 1, or by model type.
5. **How is a skill tested?** A skill should be run against real modeling
   tasks before anyone relies on it. One option is a small set of
   example datasets, each with the checks a good run should report.

## 7. First Steps

1. Build the first reference list, a couple of sources per topic, and check
   each entry against its source.
2. Pick one internal guidance document and draft the checklist it reduces to,
   to see what clearance involves.
3. Write a first skill for one topic, model evaluation being the narrowest, and
   run it on an example dataset.
4. Ask two or three people whether they would join the review group.
